summary: For ages 12–14, this topic teaches hazard assessment and evacuation as a judgement under uncertainty with competing human values. Two intertwined payloads: (1) a quantitative strand — probability is not prediction: recurrence intervals and fault slip rates give a likelihood or return period, not a date; observatories translate ground deformation, gas emissions and seismicity into staged alert levels; volcanoes and severe weather usually give precursors (so alerts are possible) while earthquakes strike without notice; and (2) a human/ethical strand — evacuation carries asymmetric costs (a false alarm brings economic loss and eroded trust; a missed warning costs lives), people stay near hazards for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture), and disaster risk falls unequally. The core activity is an in-role deliberation reaching a defensible position rather than a single correct answer, supported by quantitative risk-literacy practice.
misconceptions: 'Scientists can predict exactly when a volcano/earthquake will strike.' — Assessment yields probabilities and (for volcanoes) precursor-based alerts; earthquakes are not yet predictable — probability is not a date.
'A 1-in-100-year event won't happen for 100 years / just happened so we're safe.' — Return periods are long-run averages; the event can occur in any year, including consecutive years.
'People who live in hazard zones are just ignorant or foolish.' — They usually stay for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture); dismissing this misreads the whole risk problem.
'The safe choice is always to evacuate.' — Evacuation has real costs (economic, health, trust); false alarms erode compliance with future warnings — the decision is a genuine trade-off.
'Natural disasters affect everyone equally.' — Risk is socially uneven; the poorest and most marginalised bear disproportionate exposure and have the fewest means to prepare or recover.
'Monitoring/technology removes the risk.' — It reduces and informs, but cannot eliminate uncertainty; decisions must still be made without knowing the outcome.

activities.title: The evacuation call: reasoning in role under uncertainty
steps: Take the role of a volcano-observatory scientist briefing a mayor: the monitoring data is ambiguous — gas emissions and tremor are rising, but could fizzle out. State out loud whether to recommend evacuation and justify it.

Respond when the mayor presses back in role: 'If I evacuate 40,000 people and nothing happens, I've wrecked the harvest, cost millions, and no one will believe the next warning — are you sure?' Articulate that this is a probability, not a prophecy.
Face a lifelong resident who refuses to leave — this volcanic soil feeds their family and their grandparents are buried here. Engage their reasons seriously rather than dismissing them.
Hear an aid worker point out that it is usually the poorest, with nowhere to go, who die; factor equity into the position you defend.
Weigh the false-alarm cost (economic loss, eroded trust, 'cry wolf') against the missed-warning cost (lives) explicitly, naming that there is no cost-free choice.
Reach and defend a justified position, acknowledging you might be wrong either way.
activities.insight: Hazard assessment is not a calculation that outputs an answer; it is a judgement made under irreducible uncertainty, shaped by fairness and human stakes. One can make a good decision given the available information and still have an unlucky outcome.

activities.title: Risk dashboard: probability is not prediction
steps: Read a recurrence-interval / probability readout and a set of monitoring signals (deformation, gas, seismicity) that climb over time.
Set an alert level (e.g. green → yellow → orange → red) by mapping the monitoring signals to staged actions.
Make an evacuation call, then see a simulated outcome reveal whether the event actually came that run.
Repeat the call across many runs and watch a running tally accumulate false alarms versus missed warnings, so the cost asymmetry is felt statistically rather than argued abstractly.
Toggle a vulnerability-map overlay (hazard zone with population, poverty and infrastructure) to see that exposure and vulnerability, not hazard alone, shape who is at risk.
activities.insight: A '1-in-100-year' figure is a long-run average and an annual likelihood, not a countdown; with imperfect prediction and the same monitoring information, lowering the alert threshold to cut missed warnings raises false alarms, and raising it does the reverse, so the best alert policy manages their asymmetric costs (better monitoring can reduce both, but not to zero).

activities.title: Reading the probability and the alert ladder (factual check)
steps: Interpret statements like 'a 1-in-100 chance each year': decide whether elapsed time since the last event raises this year's chance. As a modelling assumption for this probability-literacy lesson, treat the annual chance as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time, so it does not rise simply because time has passed.
Match monitoring signals (ground deformation, gas, seismicity) to the appropriate alert level on the ladder.

Identify which hazards usually give precursors (volcanoes, severe weather) versus which strike without notice (earthquakes), and state the consequence for how each is managed (forecasting and alerts plus preparedness vs preparedness alone).
Use a tap-to-reveal vulnerability map or alert-level ladder as a reference for what each alert level means and what makes a community vulnerable.
activities.insight: Core probability literacy and monitoring facts underpin the judgement work: a return period is an average, not a schedule, and alert levels are a translation of data into staged action.

checkQuestion: A volcano observatory says a volcano has 'about a 1-in-100 chance of a major eruption each year, and on average it erupts roughly every 100 years. The last big eruption was 100 years ago.' A newspaper prints: 'Scientists say the volcano is now overdue and will erupt this year.' Is the newspaper right, and how should we understand that '1-in-100 each year'?
checkAnswer: The newspaper is wrong. A 1-in-100 annual chance is a probability, not a countdown — the volcano is not 'saving up' an eruption, and this year's risk is still about 1-in-100 no matter how long it has been. 'Every 100 years on average' is a long-run average across many unequal gaps, not a due date; each year is roughly independent.
